strengths: PCD addresses a relevant practical question: how far away a detector can meet a specified quality and reliability requirement. Expressing performance in meters provides an interpretable complement to aggregate detection metrics.

The controlled clear/rain acquisition, specified rainfall intensity of 64 mm/h, and manually annotated target provide a useful focused test setting. Evaluating five detectors without fine-tuning offers evidence that the proposed analysis is applicable across different architectures.

Table 3 illustrates potentially useful distinctions: Grounding DINO and DyHead have similar clear-weather mAP (0.564 versus 0.560), but different mPCD values (92.783 versus 73.110 meters). The threshold surfaces also make the dependence on user requirements explicit.
weaknesses: The variance estimation has substantive inconsistencies. Equation (6) subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation rather than the corresponding fitted mean f(x_i), so the stated change-point test includes distance-dependent mean variation. Equation (9) then estimates conditional noise using the standard deviation of raw segment observations, again mixing mean trends with residual variability. These directly affect the probabilities defining PCD. Even if Equation (6) is a notation error, the manuscript does not establish that the reported results use a consistent residual-based estimator.

Equation (10) does not establish the claimed maximum distance within which detection remains reliable: it selects the farthest qualifying point even if closer distances fail the requirement. Neither the spline nor the segment-dependent variance guarantees monotonic exceedance probabilities. Consequently, an isolated distant qualifying region can produce an optimistic range despite intervening unreliable regions.

The probabilistic reliability interpretation is not validated. IoU times confidence is bounded and Figure 4 shows substantial mass at zero, whereas Equation (9) assumes Gaussian observations. Sequential frames also challenge the independent-error assumption. There are no distribution diagnostics, held-out exceedance-frequency checks, or uncertainty intervals for PCD. More variance change points, as interpreted in Section 5.2.1, do not by themselves establish worse reliability; their count does not measure variance magnitude or detection success.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of uncertainty modeling and change-point detection over simpler distance-conditioned evaluation. In Figure 5, p_t = 0.5 makes the Gaussian exceedance criterion equivalent to f(x) > y_t for positive variance, so this central example is insensitive to the estimated variance. No comparison against a mean-only spline, constant-variance model, or empirical distance-binned success rate establishes that the proposed statistical machinery improves reliability assessment.

Cross-model mPCD comparisons conflate detection quality with confidence-score scaling. A monotonic rescaling of confidence can preserve predicted boxes and AP rankings while changing IoU times confidence and mPCD substantially. The paper does not examine calibration or establish whether the ranking differences in Table 3 reflect better detection range rather than different score scales. Selecting only the highest-confidence car box also leaves false-alarm behavior outside the proposed reliability assessment.

The evidence consists of 278 clear and 317 rainy images of one sedan, with no reported independent-run variability or repeatability analysis. The conditions also cover different distance ranges, approximately 214 versus 241 meters, which matters for a maximum-distance statistic averaged over permissive thresholds. This limited setting is valuable as a case study, but does not validate the broader stability claims. Reproduction is further limited by missing details on distance ground-truth acquisition, exact mPCD averaging, and handling empty qualifying sets or zero-variance segments. Overall, the useful evaluation idea is outweighed by unresolved estimator correctness and validation concerns, supporting weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful evaluation question: at what distance does a detector satisfy a specified quality and reliability requirement? Expressing performance in meters offers an interpretable complement to aggregate AP for autonomous-driving applications.

SensorRainFall provides a controlled clear-versus-rain comparison, with a specified rainfall rate of 64 mm/h and manually annotated target boxes. Such controlled acquisition can support analysis that is difficult with observational driving datasets.

Experiments cover five detectors without fine-tuning and provide distance-dependent plots and threshold sweeps. Table 3 gives a concrete example of complementary information: Grounding DINO and DyHead have similar clear-weather mAP, but their reported mPCDs differ substantially.
weaknesses: The central uncertainty estimator is not technically justified as written. Equation (9) estimates conditional standard deviation using std(y_A), the standard deviation of raw scores across a segment, rather than residuals around the distance-dependent mean. Consequently, even a perfectly predictable declining score curve can acquire substantial estimated uncertainty. Equation (6) likewise subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation rather than f(x_i), conflicting with the stated detrending model. The latter could be a notation error, but the manuscript does not establish that the reported probabilities use a correct implementation. These concerns directly affect the main contribution.

The probabilistic reliability interpretation lacks validation. IoU times confidence is bounded in [0,1], and Figure 4 shows substantial masses at zero, yet Equation (9) assumes Gaussian observations without distribution checks or empirical coverage evaluation. Sequential frames are also treated as independent errors without examining temporal dependence. No repeated-run or held-out assessment establishes that a nominal probability threshold corresponds to the observed success frequency, and no uncertainty intervals are reported for PCD.

Equation (10) selects the farthest individually qualifying distance; it does not require all shorter distances to qualify. With a nonmonotonic fitted mean or changing variance, it can bridge unreliable regions, so it does not establish the claimed maximum distance within which detection remains reliable. Furthermore, the method models marginal score variation with distance, not temporal failure duration or ordering, limiting its interpretation as a measure of temporal stability.

The experiments illustrate the metric but do not establish the benefit of its statistical machinery. There are no comparisons against distance-binned detection success, a mean-curve threshold crossing, or constant-variance estimation. In the main Figure 5 example, p_t = 0.5 makes the Gaussian exceedance criterion equivalent to a threshold on the fitted mean, independent of positive variance. Table 3 also shows weather degradation in conventional metrics, so the stronger claim that static metrics overlook these differences is insufficiently supported. Counting more variance change points, as in Section 5.2.1, does not by itself demonstrate lower reliability.

The evidence is narrow for the claimed general reliability assessment: 278 clear and 317 rainy images of one red sedan, with one rainfall intensity and no reported independent-run analysis. The distance distributions and maximum ranges also differ between conditions. This matters because spline estimates and maximum-distance summaries can depend on sampling and observed range. More fundamentally, averaging thresholds on uncalibrated confidence scores can change model rankings under score rescaling without changing localization or confidence ordering; the paper does not separate this effect from improved range reliability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful architecture and spline settings. The manuscript does not adequately specify distance-ground-truth acquisition and accuracy, independent recording runs, spline knot placement, minimum change-point segment sizes, or handling of empty qualifying sets and zero-variance segments. The exact mPCD averaging protocol is also insufficiently formalized. These reporting gaps are secondary to the estimator and validation problems: the controlled dataset and interpretable evaluation objective have merit, but the current evidence does not support the central claim of statistically reliable perception distance, which determines my weak-reject recommendation.

strengths: PCD addresses a useful practical question: how far away can a detector satisfy a specified detection-quality requirement with a specified probability? Reporting this quantity in meters offers an interpretable complement to aggregate AP.

SensorRainFall provides a controlled clear-versus-rain comparison with manually annotated targets and reported distances. Controlling rainfall at 64 mm/h is valuable for studying environmental effects on perception.

Experiments cover five detector families without fine-tuning. Table 3 illustrates potentially useful distinctions: Grounding DINO and DyHead have similar clear-weather mAP (0.564 versus 0.560), but different mPCD values (92.783 versus 73.110 meters). The threshold surfaces also help explain the proposed metric.
weaknesses: The central variance estimation is technically problematic as written. Equation (6) subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation rather than its fitted mean f(x_i), while Equation (9) estimates conditional standard deviation using raw segment scores rather than detrended residuals. Both can conflate systematic distance-dependent decline with uncertainty. Even if Equation (6) is a notation error, Equation (9) leaves a substantive concern about the probabilities underlying PCD.

The claimed statistical reliability is not validated. Scores are bounded in [0,1], and Figure 4 contains substantial zero-valued observations, yet the method assumes Gaussian distributions and independent errors without diagnostics or calibration tests. Sequential frames may be correlated, and recursive change-point testing has no reported multiplicity control. No held-out exceedance-frequency evaluation or uncertainty intervals establish that the estimated probabilities match observed reliability.

Equation (10) identifies the farthest individual distance satisfying the probability threshold; it does not ensure that all shorter distances satisfy it. With nonmonotonic fits or variance changes, an isolated distant interval can determine PCD despite unreliable nearer intervals. Thus, the definition does not establish the claimed maximum range within which detection remains consistently reliable.

The evidence does not isolate the benefit of the proposed statistical machinery. There are no comparisons against distance-binned recall, empirical exceedance rates, a mean-only spline, or constant-variance estimates. The highlighted example in Figure 5 uses p_t = 0.5, where Gaussian exceedance reduces to whether the fitted mean exceeds y_t, independently of variance. Moreover, more variance change points do not inherently imply worse reliability, contrary to the interpretation of Table 2.

Cross-model mPCD comparisons depend directly on confidence-score scaling. A monotonic recalibration can change IoU-times-confidence and mPCD while preserving boxes and confidence ranking. The manuscript neither measures calibration nor separates this effect from improved detection range, limiting the interpretation of differences between conventional and language-conditioned detectors.

The dataset contains only 595 images of one red sedan in two conditions, with different distance distributions and maximum ranges. Repeated independent runs, matched-distance comparisons, and sampling uncertainty are not reported. Consequently, the results support a narrow case study rather than broad claims about dynamic perception robustness. Selecting only the highest-confidence car prediction also leaves false-alarm behavior largely outside the evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not adequately specify distance-ground-truth acquisition and accuracy, the exact mPCD averaging procedure, or handling of empty feasible sets and zero-variance segments. These omissions are secondary to the statistical concerns, but further impede verification. Overall, the useful evaluation objective and controlled dataset provide worthwhile merits, while unresolved estimator correctness and insufficient validation of reliability favor weak rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful evaluation problem: aggregate detection metrics do not directly communicate the distance at which perception becomes unreliable. Expressing performance in meters, with adjustable quality and probability thresholds, offers an interpretable complement to AP.

SensorRainFall provides controlled adverse-weather imagery with bounding boxes, instance masks, and measured target distances. Holding target identity and scene largely fixed enables focused comparisons across environmental conditions.

The experiments cover ten perception models, two tasks, and four environmental conditions. Tables 7–10 provide comprehensive results, while Figures 5–6 illustrate concrete disagreements between aPCD and conventional rankings.
The manuscript provides spline parameters, model configuration details, and synthetic change-point experiments with 1,000 replications, offering useful methodological transparency.
weaknesses: The central reliability interpretation is not established. Equation (2) selects the farthest distance satisfying the probability threshold; it does not require all shorter distances to satisfy it. With unconstrained splines and changing variances, disconnected reliable regions are possible. Thus, this definition does not support the claimed reliable range 'within' PCD or the safety envelope described in Section 5.2. No held-out probability calibration or downstream safety validation is reported.

The variance formulation contains consequential inconsistencies. Equation (1) estimates standard deviation from raw scores within a segment, confounding the distance-dependent mean trend with residual variability. Equation (7) subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation rather than its fitted mean f(x_i), contradicting the stated detrending procedure. These may include notation errors, but the manuscript does not establish which estimator generated the results.

The Gaussian, independent-error assumptions are insufficiently justified for bounded IoU × confidence scores from sequential frames. Figure 6 shows substantial point mass at zero and spline predictions below zero, making the distributional mismatch concrete. The synthetic Gaussian experiments assess change-point counts, rather than calibration of the resulting PCD probabilities on real data, and do not address temporal dependence.

Evidence that aPCD measures stability beyond mean score and confidence scaling is weak. Multiplying by uncalibrated confidence allows score transformations to change PCD without improving localization or detection ranking. No calibration analysis, mean-only ablation, constant-variance baseline, or comparison with empirical distance-binned detection rates isolates the proposed uncertainty modeling. Different rankings alone do not establish better reliability assessment; the highlighted Example 3 difference is only 23.547 versus 23.448 m, without uncertainty estimates.

The protocol retains only the highest-confidence prediction for each target class, so additional false positives are not explicitly penalized by PCD. This limits its ability to support the operational claims about trustworthy predictions and false-positive-sensitive control. Moreover, the stated use of the prompt 'car' for both vision-language models leaves their pedestrian evaluation unclear.

Reproducibility and environmental attribution remain uncertain. The main paper specifies 64 mm/h rainfall, whereas the supplement describes 20 and 40 mm/h without reconciling the evaluated subset. The aPCD averaging grid, weighting, and handling of empty qualifying-distance sets are not clearly specified. The dataset contains only 1,231 sequential images of two physical targets, with different distance distributions across conditions and no reported independent-run uncertainty; this particularly limits claims of statistically reliable environmental comparisons.

strengths: PCD addresses a useful practical question: at what distance does perception meet a specified detection-quality requirement with a specified probability? Reporting performance in meters provides an interpretable complement to AP.

SensorRainFall offers controlled weather and illumination comparisons, with 1,231 images, distance measurements, bounding boxes, and instance masks. This is a potentially useful resource for studying distance-dependent degradation.

The evaluation covers ten perception models across two tasks, two targets, and four conditions. The supplementary tables provide detailed results, and the synthetic experiments investigate sample-size and variance-shift effects.
weaknesses: The statistical specification has consequential inconsistencies. Equation (1) estimates segment uncertainty from the standard deviation of raw scores, which mixes distance-dependent mean variation with noise. Equation (7) subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation rather than its fitted mean f(x_i), contrary to the stated residual-based procedure. These could be correctable errors, but the manuscript does not establish which estimator produced the results.

The Gaussian probability model is not validated on real observations. IoU times confidence is bounded in [0,1], and Figure 6 shows substantial zero inflation, while sequential images also challenge the independent-error assumption. Gaussian simulations do not establish calibrated exceedance probabilities on these data; consequently, the probabilistic reliability interpretation remains unsupported.

Equation (2) selects the farthest qualifying distance without requiring all shorter distances to qualify. Neither spline fitting nor segmentwise variance enforces monotonic reliability. Thus, the definition does not establish the claimed reliable interval or safety envelope. Moreover, a 0.5 exceedance threshold cannot justify Section 5.2's description of operation 'without risking perception failures.'

The evidence for aPCD's added value is largely qualitative and self-referential: ranking differences are explained using the same confidence-weighted scores that define the metric. Confidence rescaling can change aPCD without changing boxes or confidence rankings, but cross-model calibration is not examined. Comparisons against distance-binned recall, empirical exceedance curves, or a mean-only estimator are absent. Example 3's 23.547 versus 23.448 m difference is interpreted without uncertainty estimates.

The stability claim needs qualification. Under the Gaussian model, increasing variance can increase the exceedance probability when the mean is below the quality threshold; low probability thresholds can therefore reward variability. Figures 5–6 use p=0.3, but the paper does not analyze this behavior or establish how averaging thresholds preserves a preference for stability. Selecting only the highest-confidence prediction per class also leaves additional false positives outside the proposed metric.

Dataset scope and reporting limit the environmental conclusions. The experiments use one sedan and one surrogate pedestrian, without reported independent-run uncertainty, and condition-specific distance distributions differ substantially in Table 2. Section 3 specifies 64 mm/h rainfall, whereas the supplement specifies 20 and 40 mm/h. The exact aPCD integration grid, weighting, and empty-set handling are also unspecified. These issues affect interpretation and reproducibility rather than merely presentation.

Overall, the interpretable distance-based objective and controlled dataset are worthwhile, but unresolved estimator correctness and insufficient validation of the reliability interpretation currently outweigh those merits. The recommendation is driven by these central issues, not by limited benchmark breadth alone.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful evaluation problem: aggregate AP does not directly describe the distance at which perception becomes unreliable. PCD expresses performance in meters at explicit quality and probability thresholds, which could make it a useful complement to conventional metrics.

SensorRainFall provides a valuable controlled experimental setting, with bounding boxes, instance masks, and measured target distances under four weather/illumination conditions. Holding target identities and the test environment relatively fixed helps investigate environmental effects.

The experiments cover ten models across detection and segmentation, with detailed supplementary results. Table 1 and Figures 5–6 illustrate concrete disagreements between aPCD and AP rankings, motivating further investigation of distance-dependent evaluation.

The manuscript provides substantial methodological detail and synthetic experiments examining sample size and variance-change magnitude, rather than presenting the metric solely through benchmark rankings.
weaknesses: The central reliability interpretation is insufficiently validated. Equation (1) assumes Gaussian conditional scores, although IoU × confidence is bounded and Figures 5–6 show substantial point masses at zero. Sequential observations also challenge the independent-error assumption. There are no held-out checks showing that an estimated probability threshold corresponds to the observed detection frequency. Consequently, the claimed probabilistic reliability is a modeling assumption rather than an established property.

The statistical specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Equation (1) estimates segment variance using raw scores, which mixes distance-dependent changes in the mean with residual variability. Equation (7) subtracts f(x_tau) from every observation instead of its own fitted mean f(x_i), despite the preceding residual-model formulation. Equation (8) also uses likelihood arguments inconsistently with Equation (7). These may include correctable notation errors, but the manuscript does not establish which estimator produced the results, and the ambiguity directly affects the proposed metric.

Equation (2) selects the farthest point satisfying the probability criterion; it does not require the criterion to hold at every shorter distance. Neither the spline mean nor the resulting exceedance probabilities are constrained to be monotonic. Thus, this definition does not establish the reliable interior region claimed in Section 5.2. Describing a threshold of 0.5 as an envelope within which perception can be trusted 'without risking perception failures' further overstates what the definition supports.

The comparison does not isolate reliability from confidence scaling. Multiplying IoU by uncalibrated model confidence allows score rescaling to change aPCD without changing boxes, masks, or detection rankings. No calibration analysis establishes cross-model comparability. Moreover, retaining only the highest-confidence prediction per target class excludes most false positives, so the benchmark cannot substantiate the discussion of precision and false-positive-sensitive operational choices.

Ranking disagreements alone do not demonstrate that aPCD better captures stability. There is no comparison with empirical distance-binned success rates, a simpler distance-conditioned estimator, or an ablation removing variance-change detection. The highlighted Example 3 advantage is only 23.547 versus 23.448 meters, without uncertainty estimates. Synthetic studies evaluate change-point behavior under Gaussian simulations but do not validate the final metric on real observations or its relationship to downstream safety.

The dataset scope and reproducibility leave meaningful uncertainty. The 1,231 images contain only one sedan and one surrogate pedestrian at one facility, with no reported run-level variability analysis. Section 3 specifies 64 mm/h rainfall, whereas the supplement describes nominal rates of 20 and 40 mm/h. The aPCD integration bounds, grid, and normalization are not explicitly specified. These issues matter more than editorial refinements because they affect replication and interpretation of the reported distances. Overall, the practical motivation and controlled data are worthwhile, but unresolved metric correctness and validation concerns currently outweigh the case for acceptance.
